hints: Start from the source animal - cattle are described as bovines in biology, and the human TB bacterium already tells you the genus name to keep.
walkthrough:
Link the host to the name**
You already know human TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The bacterium that causes TB in cattle belongs to the same genus, Mycobacterium, but it is a different species adapted to cattle.

Recall the bovine species**
The species name for cattle is bovis, so the bacterium transmitted from dairy cows to humans is Mycobacterium bovis. Remember to write the genus with a capital letter and the species in lower case, both in italics.

hints: Think about what routinely happens to milk between the cow and the shop that uses gentle heating to make it safe without spoiling taste - what could you do to milk from these herds?
walkthrough:
Follow the route of infection**
Here the bacteria are inside milk from infected cows. You cannot test or treat the cows, so you have to make the milk itself safe before people drink it.

Heat to kill bacteria**
Gentle heating of milk to about 72 degrees C for a short time, called pasteurisation, kills Mycobacterium and most other pathogens while keeping the milk usable. Boiling or sterilising milk would also work.
Final answer: Pasteurise milk / only drink pasteurised milk and use it for dairy products.

hints: Remember TB mainly affects the lungs - how would bacteria get out of one set of lungs and into another set of lungs?
Think about the tiny fluid particles produced when coughing or sneezing and what happens when another animal breathes nearby.
walkthrough:
Exit from the lungs**
Because M. tuberculosis infects lung tissue, it is present in the airways and lung fluids. When an infected person coughs, sneezes, talks or simply breathes out forcefully, tiny droplets of fluid containing bacteria are expelled into the air.

Entry by inhalation**
These droplets can remain suspended as aerosols or droplet infection. If an animal is close by and inhales or breathes in this contaminated air, the bacteria are drawn into its own lungs and can start infection there.
Final answer: Infected person coughs / sneezes / breathes out / talks, producing airborne droplets / aerosols containing M. tuberculosis, which are then inhaled / breathed in by the animal.

hints: TB is caused by bacteria, so think about which general type of drug kills bacteria rather than viruses, and why one drug alone often fails.
Think about why treatment must involve more than one named drug and last for many months rather than a few days.
walkthrough:
Kill bacteria with antibiotics**
Latent TB bacteria are dormant but still alive in the lungs, so antibiotics or antibacterials are needed. Vaccination will not cure an existing infection.

Use a combination for a long time**
Doctors use a combination of two or more antibiotics at the same time, for example rifampicin plus isoniazid, for about 4 to 12 months. This long combined course is needed to kill all slow-growing bacteria and to prevent antibiotic resistance developing, and it works faster than using a single antibiotic alone.
Final answer: Treatment with a combination of antibiotics, e.g. rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, taken for 4 to 12 months.

hints: Picture the wall of an elastic artery - which middle layer lets it stretch when blood surges in and then spring back?
Think about what happens to stretching and recoiling if infection destroys elastic fibres and smooth muscle in that middle layer.
Now link that weakened, overstretched wall to the very high blood pressure inside elastic arteries to explain bursting.
walkthrough:
Remember how an elastic artery works**
Elastic arteries close to the heart carry blood at very high pressure. Their thick tunica media contains lots of elastic fibres and smooth muscle for stretch and recoil, and the outer tunica externa contains tough collagen fibres for strength and to prevent over-expansion.

Damage removes stretch and strength**
M. tuberculosis infection damages the wall, destroying elastic fibres and smooth muscle in the tunica media and collagen in the tunica externa. Scar tissue may replace them, which does not stretch.

Weak wall bursts under pressure**
Without normal elastic fibres the wall cannot stretch safely and cannot recoil properly. Without collagen it cannot resist the high pressure of blood. The weakened region therefore overstretches and bulges out as an aneurysm and can then rupture or burst.

Final answer: Damage / loss of elastic fibres and smooth muscle in tunica media and damage / loss of collagen in tunica externa; wall cannot withstand high blood pressure, overstretches and shows poor recoil, leading to aneurysm and rupture.
